faq.a: Myeloablative destroys all marrow cells, requiring full donor engraftment; reduced‑intensity uses lower doses, allowing mixed chimerism and is safer for older or comorbid patients.
faq.q: What is the difference between myeloablative and reduced‑intensity conditioning?

faq.a: Allogeneic grafts contain donor immune cells that can attack host tissue (GVHD); a close HLA match minimizes this risk.
faq.q: Why is HLA matching more critical for allogeneic than autologous transplants?

faq.a: Start high‑dose systemic steroids, assess organ involvement, and add calcineurin inhibitor (e.g., tacrolimus) for synergistic immunosuppression.
faq.q: What are the first steps if a patient develops acute GVHD?

exam: A 22‑year‑old with ALL in first remission is offered BMT – which donor type gives the best disease‑free survival and why? — HLA‑matched sibling; provides graft‑versus‑leukaemia effect with lower GVHD risk.
You receive a peripheral blood CD34+ count of 1 × 10⁶/kg – what does this mean for engraftment? — Dose is suboptimal; risk of delayed engraftment, consider a second collection or marrow boost.

A patient on day +10 post‑allogeneic BMT develops fever, rash, and rising bilirubin – what is your differential and immediate management? — Consider acute GVHD vs infection; start steroids for GVHD while obtaining cultures and liver biopsy if unclear.
Why is prophylactic fluconazole given to all BMT recipients? — Prevents invasive candidiasis, a common early fungal infection in neutropenic patients.

In a low‑resource setting where PCR HLA typing is unavailable, how would you proceed with donor selection? — Use high‑resolution serology, prioritize sibling donors, and consider regional transplant centres for advanced typing.

A patient with sickle cell disease is being evaluated for BMT; what are the key eligibility criteria? — No active organ damage, adequate cardiac/pulmonary function, matched donor, and disease‑related complications outweigh transplant risk.

Explain the mechanism of graft‑versus‑leukaemia and its clinical implication. — Donor immune cells recognize residual leukaemic cells, improving relapse rates; however, it increases GVHD risk, requiring balanced immunosuppression.
What are the signs of engraftment syndrome and how is it managed? — Fever, rash, weight gain, pulmonary infiltrates around day +7–14; treat with short‑course steroids while monitoring for infection.
ai.title: Bone Marrow Transplantation
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Bone marrow transplantation (BMT) replaces diseased hematopoietic tissue with healthy stem cells. It is used for malignant and non‑malignant hematologic disorders, with curative intent when other therapies fail.

sections.p: BMT involves harvesting hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) from donor marrow, peripheral blood, or cord blood and infusing them after the recipient receives a conditioning regimen that eradicates diseased marrow and suppresses immunity.

t.b: Is a suitable donor available? – A high‑resolution match (≥8/8) reduces graft‑versus‑host disease (GVHD).
Is the stem‑cell dose adequate? – ≥2 × 10⁶ CD34+ cells/kg predicts engraftment.

b: Engraftment: ANC >500/µL and platelet >20 000/µL for three consecutive days
Acute GVHD: skin rash, jaundice, diarrhea within 100 days
Chronic GVHD: scleroderma‑like skin changes, dry eyes, bronchiolitis obliterans after day 100
sections.p: Engraftment, graft‑versus‑host disease, and infection risk define the clinical course. Success depends on disease status, donor match, and conditioning intensity.

t.b: Is engraftment occurring? – Cellular marrow with early myeloid precursors indicates successful graft.
Is liver GVHD present? – Rising bilirubin >2 mg/dL with skin rash suggests acute GVHD.

b: Severe aplastic anaemia unresponsive to immunosuppression
Inherited marrow failure (e.g., thalassaemia major, sickle cell disease) when curative intent is needed
sections.p: In low‑resource East African hospitals, BMT is rare, but understanding indications helps triage patients for referral and manage complications when transplant services are accessed abroad.

t.b: Is the disease in remission? – <5 % blasts in marrow for leukaemia qualifies for transplant.
Is the patient HIV‑positive? – Active HIV is a contraindication unless well‑controlled on ART.

b: Describe conditioning regimens and why reduced‑intensity is used in older patients.
List primary prophylaxis for opportunistic infections (e.g., fluconazole, acyclovir, TMP‑SMX).
Explain the rationale for donor‑derived versus autologous grafts in leukaemia.
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to plan, anticipate complications, and choose appropriate prophylaxis.

b: Assuming fever always means infection – consider engraftment syndrome.
Neglecting GVHD prophylaxis in allogeneic transplants.
Using high‑dose steroids for mild skin GVHD without biopsy confirmation.
sections.p: Pitfalls include overlooking donor‑recipient HLA mismatches, delaying infection prophylaxis, and misinterpreting early engraftment labs.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly rising bilirubin >2 mg/dL with skin rash
Severe pancytopenia beyond expected engraftment window
